strengths: The paper offers a useful empirical contribution to vision-language dataset design: it studies differences in descriptions of the same images across languages, extending beyond geographical image diversity or culturally specific object categories.

The central comparison controls image identity and caption count. Complementary results from human-annotated Crossmodal data, LLaVA, and Vertex support the narrower claim that multilingual caption sets contain more varied semantic content.

The follow-up experiments strengthen the coverage finding. In Table 3, multilingual Vertex captions cover 11.5% of Visual Genome objects versus 9.3–10.3% for individual-language sets. The study involving 20 English/Japanese speakers and 30 images also reports increased coverage, providing evidence beyond model-generated captions.

The authors make meaningful efforts to address translation and modeling concerns: a human translation audit reports 4.68/5 average quality, and fine-tuning uses equal-sized datasets with common training images and held-out evaluation images. The frequent corresponding-language performance advantages establish practical relevance to caption evaluation.
weaknesses: The interpretation exceeds what the measurements establish. Differences in selected caption content do not distinguish visual perception from linguistic conventions, reporting preferences, or annotation practices. Language-conditioned model outputs likewise do not establish inherited cultural perception. The English/Japanese study corroborates differences in descriptions, but language and country remain confounded. The acknowledged proxy limitation does not adequately support stronger conclusions such as 'perception is not objective.'

Translation validation is stronger for factual content than for expressive measurements. Preserving objects and relations does not establish preservation of LIWC authenticity, tone, or analytic style. The language classifier's 16.43% accuracy versus 14.29% chance also cannot establish that translation artifacts are absent, particularly without uncertainty estimates or a matched-content translation control. These issues materially weaken the interpretation of the expression and representation results.

The fine-tuning experiments demonstrate adaptation to annotation distributions more directly than improved visual understanding or robustness. There is no independent evaluation establishing those broader benefits. Table 17 reports mixed-test SPICE of 0.154 for French-only training versus 0.151 for multilingual training; Table 16 similarly reports 0.246 versus 0.244. These results are compatible with multilingual training being competitive, but Table 11's summary that multilingual training is best on the mixed evaluation is unsupported.

Statistical support and reproducibility are incomplete. Central coverage comparisons and fine-tuning results lack confidence intervals or repeated-run variability, which matters particularly for the smaller human-study effects and close model rankings. Scene-graph merging thresholds, precise model checkpoints, generation settings, and fine-tuning hyperparameters are insufficiently specified. The paper also does not quantify parser or canonicalization errors that could affect concept counts.

Several reporting discrepancies require an audit. Table 1 gives a Vertex monolingual attribute average of 1.98 although every component value is between 1.59 and 1.86; their mean is approximately 1.69. In Table 17, multilingual training ranks second on four language tests and first on Chinese, rather than second on five as stated. Minor notation and cross-reference errors are presentation issues; these numerical discrepancies affect confidence in the summaries. Overall, the repeated caption-diversity findings provide substantial merit, while unresolved measurement validity and evidentiary gaps keep the recommendation at the decision boundary.
